subject: chemistry
question_text: Classify the oxide PbO₂ as neutral, acidic, basic or amphoteric.

mark_split.label: The classification and the alkali reaction

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.104, chapter 9 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS GROUP 14, Very Short Answer Questions question 4(f). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book's classification of PbO₂ as amphoteric is correct and is what this card gives. THE ACID REACTION IS CONDITION-DEPENDENT and the card says so: with COLD concentrated hydrochloric acid PbO₂ + 4HCl → PbCl₄ + 2H₂O (Pb 1, O 2, H 4, Cl 4 each side), and lead(IV) chloride decomposes on warming to PbCl₂ and chlorine, which is why the hot reaction is written as PbO₂ + 4HCl → PbCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O in some books. Both are correct at their own temperature; neither is an error, and a card that printed only one without its condition would be misleading. The alkali equation PbO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂PbO₃ + H₂O has Pb 1, Na 2, H 2, O 4 on each side. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty.

steps.label: The classification and the alkali reaction
lines: Lead dioxide PbO₂ is an amphoteric oxide:
it reacts with an alkali and also with an
With a fused alkali it behaves as an

The salt is sodium plumbate Na₂PbO₃.
steps.why: Lead is the last member of group 14, and its higher oxide is amphoteric rather than acidic. That is the pattern down the group: as the element becomes more metallic, the acidic character of its oxide falls and the basic character rises, so the acidic oxides CO₂ and SiO₂ at the top of the group are matched by an amphoteric PbO₂ at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Calling PbO₂ basic because lead is a metal. It gives a plumbate with alkali, which a purely basic oxide does not do.
Writing the plumbate ion as PbO₂²⁻. In sodium plumbate Na₂PbO₃ the ion is PbO₃²⁻.
steps.memory_tip: Alkali turns lead dioxide into a plumbate, so PbO₂ has an acidic side.
steps.margin_note: Name the class first, then give the alkali equation for the acidic half.

steps.label: The reaction with an acid

steps.why: The reaction with an acid is the basic half, and it must be written before the word amphoteric can be used. Lead is more stable as +2 than as +4 because of the inert pair effect, so the lead(IV) chloride formed in the cold does not last on warming, and that same instability is why PbO₂ is used as an oxidising agent.
common_mistakes: Writing PbCl₂ as the direct product in the cold. The cold reaction gives PbCl₄; PbCl₂ and chlorine come from PbCl₄ on warming.
Answering only that PbO₂ is an oxidising agent. That is true, but the question asks for the class of the oxide, which is amphoteric.
steps.memory_tip: Alkali gives the plumbate, acid gives the chloride: PbO₂ is amphoteric.
steps.margin_note: Both halves are needed; the acid reaction is the one usually left out.

insider_note: Lead dioxide is amphoteric and is also a strong oxidising agent, and the two are easy to confuse. The class asked for is amphoteric; the oxidising power explains why its lead(IV) products do not last on warming.
